title: The Scandal at 1612 Prairie
premise: A carriage manufacturer's showplace has become the most scrutinized residence on the block: a society divorce, a judicial order, a violin in a disabled automobile, and a small boy positioned at the center of everything.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE SCANDAL AT 1612 PRAIRIE. A Monday afternoon in November 1904, at the tranquil northern extremity of Prairie Avenue.

Four stops along a single short block. The residence at 1612 has served as a showplace for twenty years; this year it has become a battlefield. A husband has initiated litigation, a judge has awarded the residence to the wife, and in November the husband stood in open court and leveled accusations that the entire city has subsequently consumed in the Tribune. The neighbors keep their curtains drawn and their attention acutely engaged.

Begin next door, where you can envision the residence as it formerly appeared.

stops.text: 1608 Prairie, and adjoining it the substantial square residence at 1612. Two decades ago it belonged to a Studebaker, of the Studebaker Brothers carriage works, and it was the most resplendent house on the avenue. In February 1884 approximately two hundred guests arrived from a family wedding, and "the large residence was brilliantly illuminated, and every room was elaborately decorated with smilax and cut flowers". An 1887 society column documented the traffic: "Morning and night, a showy turnout is noticed before the squarely-built house, with the number 1612 over the portals". A carriage manufacturer's residence ought to exhibit the finest equipages at its entrance, and it did. Observe it now: no carriage waits at the curb, and a neighboring maid monitors it from her steps. Walk to the gate of 1612.

stage.caption: A maid at 1608 sweeps her steps while maintaining vigilant surveillance of the residence next door.

stops.text: 1612 Prairie. The Tribune possesses the story, as does everyone else. Last May the husband, Charles E. Brown, petitioned for divorce. His wife Catherine is twenty-seven, "the daughter of Gen. Graves, a wealthy resident of Buffalo", and the stated grounds were "habitual drunkenness and statutory charges". Judge Tuley subsequently granted Mrs. Brown possession of this residence, which she, her husband and their son had occupied, together with $200 monthly in temporary alimony pending resolution. Consequently the wife occupies the fortress while the husband remains excluded. Behind those windows reside a woman whom the newspapers have rendered notorious and a small boy. The residence will survive until its demolition around 1960. Proceed next door to learn what the husband alleged in November.

stage.caption: A lady emerges onto the porch of 1612, surveys the avenue in both directions, and withdraws before anyone can approach her.

cast.name: Catherine G. Brown (no card in the town; an unnamed figure plays her)

stops.text: 1616 Prairie, the adjacent residence to the south, where the neighbors peruse the Tribune over coffee. In November Mr. Brown returned to court, alleging that his wife "had conducted herself in a disgraceful manner, had been habitually intoxicated, and had done many freakish things, such as playing a violin in a broken automobile while a man pushed the machine along a public highway, and dancing about the rear of their home clothed only in a nightrobe". He additionally identified "E. C. Edsall, an automobile salesman", with whom, the husband asserted, she absconded to an eastern summer resort and subsequently to New York City. It constitutes the most sensational scandal on Prairie Avenue in years, and two maids are relishing it. Yet a divorce never concerns only two individuals. Look for the boy.

stage.caption: Two maids on the steps of 1616 share the newspaper and cast glances toward 1612.

stops.text: Across the avenue at 1613, look back at the western side of the block. The boy is Charles Edward Brown, the couple's only son, and he represents the genuine prize in this contest. A nurse escorts him along the sidewalk past his own entrance; his mother retains the residence, whereas his father seeks its recovery, and his. The court has not yet ruled. In newspaper columns he appears merely as a concluding sentence, but on this walk he is the sole participant in the entire affair who has done absolutely nothing. The Tribune will report the resolution in March 1905, by which time the residence, the boy and the woman will each have followed divergent paths.

stage.caption: A nurse escorts a small boy along the far sidewalk past the entrance of 1612, and he pauses to gaze up at it.

cast.name: Charles Edward Brown, the son (no card in the town; an unnamed figure plays him)

endings.text: The walk concludes here. Following a bitter contest early in 1905, the husband prevailed, obtaining the divorce, the Prairie Avenue property and custody of the boy. On 8 March 1905 he conveyed the property to Charles Palmerston Anderson, the Episcopal bishop of Chicago. That same week the Tribune located Catherine Brown in a police cell, arrested at 3667 Wabash Avenue, where police reported she had been living as Kittie Casey, and fined $85 for disorderly conduct. "I am penniless", she declared. "I cannot pay the fine". From her cell she reflected, "It's all because a woman is jealous of me, I guess". The general's daughter from Buffalo had retained 1612 Prairie for less than a year, and the newspapers that manufactured her notoriety recorded almost exclusively her husband's allegations, a reminder to read every such account with deliberate skepticism.

keepsake.title: The 1612 Court Papers
keepsake.text: An interpretive card documenting the Brown divorce of 1904 and 1905 as the Tribune reported it; a reconstruction prepared for this walk, not a historical artifact.

evidence.text: On 21 February 1884 about 200 of the intimate friends and relatives of the bride and groom were received at the residence of W. F. Studebaker, No. 1612 Prairie avenue, after the Studebaker-Innis wedding. 'The large residence was brilliantly illuminated, and every room was elaborately decorated with smilax and cut flowers.'
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 22 February 1884, 'Wedding Bells', as transcribed.

evidence.text: Inter Ocean, 2 January 1887: 'Morning and night, a showy turnout is noticed before the squarely-built house, with the number 1612 over the portals.' Its owner was one of the Studebaker Brothers, the carriage makers.

The Scandal at 1612 Prairie: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Scandal at 1612 Prairie: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

Catherine G. Brown was the 'former wife of Charles E. Brown, 1612 Prairie avenue'. Mrs. Brown, who is 27 years old and the daughter of Gen. Graves, a wealthy resident of Buffalo, first attracted notoriety in May, 1904, when her husband filed a bill for divorce. By a court order issued by Judge Tuley Mrs. Brown was given possession of the residence, 1612 Prairie avenue, where she and her husband and their son had lived, and was granted temporary alimony amounting to $200 a month while the suit was pending. Habitual drunkenness and statutory charges were the grounds.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, 'Story of Divorce Case', as transcribed.

evidence.text: Joseph Goodman Residence, 1612 S. Prairie Avenue: razed circa 1960.

In November Mr. Brown appeared in court and charged that his wife had conducted herself in a disgraceful manner, had been habitually intoxicated, and had done many freakish things, such as playing a violin in a broken automobile while a man pushed the machine along a public highway, and dancing about the rear of their home clothed only in a nightrobe.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, 'Story of Divorce Case', as transcribed.

evidence.text: He also charged her with receiving the attentions of E. C. Edsall, an automobile salesman. With Edsall, the husband charged, Mrs. Brown ran away to an eastern summer resort and later to New York City.
After a bitter fight Mr. Brown was granted a divorce about six weeks before 11 March 1905, and given possession of the Prairie avenue property, and the custody of the one son, Charles Edward Brown.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, the last paragraph, as transcribed.

evidence.text: In March 1905 Mrs. Catherine G. Brown was arrested at 3667 Wabash avenue, where she had been living under the name of Kittie Casey, according to the police, and fined $85 for disorderly conduct. 'I am penniless,' she said. 'I cannot pay the fine.' In her cell she said: 'It's all because a woman is jealous of me, I guess.' Justice Hurley called her 'a problem in humanity to me.'
On 8 March 1905 the lot at 1612 Prairie passed from Brown (printed 'Chas. S. Brown') to the Rt. Rev. Chas. Palmerston Anderson, bishop of the Protestant Episcopal church in the diocese of Chicago.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 14 March 1905, the transfer list, as transcribed.
